about: The committed matrix of docs/upstream-parity.md (decision D6): each cell holds an image of wz to the original built by this repository, with the verdict of decision D1 (WIN, TIE or LOSS; only WIN counts). The rows of a run are the output of `scripts/lib/kit_compare.py --format rows` for that run, never figures copied by hand; a change that moves a cell moves its run here, in the same commit, with the run that measured it.

runs.target: mcu-zephyr: the T2G kit (CYT4BF, Cortex-M7 at 350 MHz) on its own Ethernet to a zenohd 1.10.0 with its REST plugin on the bench host
runs.workload: W1: answer the two GETs of the wz client's keys, 2,000 times each per boot, through the router
runs.reference: zephyr-pico-queryable-st: zenoh-pico with the wz client's planes (queryable, UDP unicast) in its single-threaded arm, the stronger of its two arms in every cell of this run
runs.method: scripts/kit-lane.sh compare --boots 24, compare builds (CONFIG_WZ_MEMORY_REPORT), images alternated per round, turnaround read at the host's wire
runs.tree: origin's main at 609e7b5c21 (the SCE pin at dc579571aa, zenoh-pico at 1.10.2 as the reference, the kernel heap pools of both images stated by the quarter-free rule: the wz heap client 11,264 bytes, zenoh-pico 13,312 in both arms); sent to the bench host. The run before it was of the same tree but for the ledger commits
caveats: Two programs written for one workload, the same keys, bodies and encoding on the wire (decision D4): the cells move to pico's own programs on both libraries when the pico C ABI runs on the MCU (step M5).

The ram cell holds each image's static RAM, which includes its kernel heap pool. Both pools are stated by the rule HW.7 holds a main stack to, a quarter free (peak * 4 <= pool * 3): the wz heap client 11,264 bytes (it ran with 9,216, the least tried, at its heap peak of 8,412 then) and zenoh-pico 13,312 in both arms (the single-threaded arm answered with 9,728 and did not answer with 9,216; both searches were made at zenoh-pico 1.10.1, and the boots of this run ran at 1.10.2 with these pools; the multi-threaded arm's least was not searched). Both pools were 131,072 until the run before. The fixed client takes nothing from the heap and has none.

Both sides of this run poll the receive path out of the ITCM (CONFIG_WZ_POLL_PATH_IN_ITCM). The turnaround of the fixed client reads 0.1879 ms and the heap client's 0.1900 against 0.1960 for the single-threaded pico: the ratios, 0.9586 (interval 0.9540 to 0.9599) and 0.9696 (0.9642 to 0.9696), twenty-four boots of each image, are WIN for both. The runs before were of twelve boots. The boots of one image spread about 0.012 ms, which put the interval of a ratio of twelve against twelve at about 3 percent on each side, and the number was moved to twenty-four for that reason, before this run was read: the run before it read the heap client's ratio at 0.9875 (interval 0.9478 to 1.0097), a TIE, and the two before that WIN. The medians of the heap client and the fixed client, one code but for where the storage block is, differ by +2.1 microseconds here (heap minus fixed; +0.5, -2.3 and +8.1 in the three runs before).

The text cells are of the compare builds, which carry the memory report: the fixed client reads 143,620 bytes here and 142,528 in the build the kit lane's text gate holds (deploy/text_budget.json), 1,092 more; the heap client 143,552 against 142,452, 1,100 more. The reference reads 144,844 bytes.

The stack_used cell is the difference of two sums of thread readings, and only the difference is the cell's; each reading is the worst of the boots. The wz clients read 5,652 against the reference's 5,820, 168 bytes (2.9 percent) under. The receive queue thread of the network stack, Zephyr's, reads 496 in all three images (the reference read 368 in the runs of twelve boots before: the worst of more boots is not less), so the cell is the main thread's, 2,720 against 2,888; the wz clients' main thread reads the receive of a handshake message, not a query's answer. The margin was 40 bytes in the runs before and was the reference's thread reading low.

The heap_peak cell of the heap client is its storage block, 8,224 bytes, taken from the kernel heap at start, and the allocator's own 28: 8,252 bytes against the reference's 9,280. The block was 11,568 bytes before the batch, the reply limit, the queues and the delayed-send queues of the two machines were stated by what the client carries (a batch of 1,024 bytes and replies of 96 are this firmware's numbers: the documents it answers with are 63 and 72 bytes, and a router takes the smaller of its batch and the node's).

The margins are small: text 1,224 bytes (0.85 percent) for the fixed client and 1,292 (0.89) for the heap client, flash 1,320 and 1,388, stack_used 168 bytes (2.9 percent), ram 9,077 (7.9 percent) and 6,597 (5.7), and the turnaround intervals end 4.0 and 3.0 percent under 1. Text and flash are of deterministic builds, so they hold until a change moves them; a change is read against these margins and not against the verdict.

The text and the instruction-cache layout move together on this kit: the same source read 41.4 and 42.0 us in the stamps with 392 bytes of unreached code between them, so a turnaround difference below a microsecond is not attributed to a source change.
